title: Two Chains, Many Hands: The Double Helix
subtitle: King's College London, the Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, and Pasadena, 1951–1953
intro: In the winter of 1952–53 the structure of DNA was worked on in three places at once. At King's College London, in a basement under the Strand, Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Raymond Gosling were taking X-ray photographs of DNA fibres and analysing them by slow, careful mathematics. Down the corridor, and on bad terms with her, Maurice Wilkins was working on the same molecule. Fifty miles away at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, Francis Crick and James Watson had been told to leave DNA to King's, and were building models anyway. In Pasadena, Linus Pauling, the most famous chemist in the world, had sent off a structure of his own.

This chapter is built mostly from notebooks, letters, typescripts and the published papers, not diaries. Franklin's laboratory notebooks and her dated draft of March 1953 survive at the Churchill Archives Centre in Cambridge, and many are online through the US National Library of Medicine. The Pauling family's letters and Linus Pauling's research notes are digitised by Oregon State University. Letters between Wilkins and Crick are at Cold Spring Harbor and King's College London. Several of the best-known scenes, though, come from accounts written much later. Watson's The Double Helix (1968) is a memoir published fifteen years on, and its portrait of Franklin has been disputed ever since. Other later sources include Gosling's interviews, Wilkins's 2003 autobiography, Perutz's 1969 letter defending himself, and Aaron Klug's analyses of Franklin's notebooks. Each of these is marked as later testimony where it is used.

The heart of the chapter is a question of timing: who knew what, and when. Two documents have carried most of the argument. One is Photograph 51, the B-form pattern taken in May 1952, which Wilkins showed Watson on 30 January 1953. The other is the December 1952 report of the King's unit to a Medical Research Council committee, which Max Perutz passed to the Cambridge pair in February 1953. Some writers have called this a theft of Franklin's data. Others, including Gosling in later life, Perutz, and the historians Matthew Cobb and Nathaniel Comfort, describe something more tangled: informal sharing within a small British community, with Franklin as an equal member of a scattered four-person effort. On this view her credit was understated rather than stolen. The book records each position and the evidence offered for it, and gives no verdict of its own.

What the notebooks do settle is that Franklin was moving under her own power. Between 19 January and 24 February 1953 her notes take her from a two-chain antiparallel A form to the conclusion that both forms are two-chain helices with the phosphates on the outside. Her draft paper is dated 17 March 1953, one day before the Watson–Crick manuscript reached King's. Klug, who knew her work best, judged that she was still a step or two short of base-pairing. The three Nature papers of 25 April 1953 were printed one after another. Their order, and the modest wording of the Cambridge paper's thanks to King's, are part of the record this chapter lays out.

Franklin died of ovarian cancer on 16 April 1958, aged 37. In 1962 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Crick, Watson and Wilkins. Nobel statutes do not allow posthumous awards, so she could not have been named whatever the committee thought. The quarrel over credit began with Watson's book in 1968 and still goes on. It is part of this story, but so is the science: a photograph, a symmetry, a set of cardboard bases, and a structure that suggested how life copies itself.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian and were written as such at the time. Where the record gives only a month, or where later accounts disagree on the day (Photo 51 is often given as 6 May 1952; the King's group's visit to the 1951 three-chain model is given variously as late November or early December), the entry is marked approx. Dates from Watson's 1968 memoir are reconstructions written fifteen years later and are marked as such.

eyes.name: Rosalind Elsie Franklin
eyes.role: Physical chemist and X-ray crystallographer, aged 30–32; Turner and Newall Research Fellow in Randall's MRC Biophysics Unit, King's College London
eyes.side: King's College London (MRC Biophysics Unit), then Birkbeck College
eyes.where: Basement X-ray laboratory beneath the Strand, London; from mid-March 1953 Birkbeck College, Torrington Square
eyes.vantage_label: principal experimenter; her photographs, measurements and notebooks underlie the structure
eyes.form: notebook (laboratory notebooks), dated typescript draft, letters, published papers
eyes.authenticity: Her laboratory notebooks, seminar notes, her notes on the Pauling–Corey paper and the typescript draft dated 17 March 1953 are in The Papers of Rosalind Franklin at the Churchill Archives Centre, Cambridge, and many are digitised in NLM Profiles in Science. Notebook dates in this chapter follow Aaron Klug's published analyses (1968, 1974, 2004) and the NLM catalogue. She left no diary. Her letter to Pauling of early 1953 is known from his reply-side correspondence.
eyes.bio: Trained at Newnham College, Cambridge, she spent the war studying the porosity of coal at the British Coal Utilisation Research Association and then four years in Paris learning X-ray diffraction of carbons. Randall brought her to King's to lead the X-ray work on DNA, a brief that Wilkins seems not to have been told about. She found the A and B forms of DNA, made the sharpest photographs of both, and worked out a good part of the structure by rigorous analysis rather than model-building. Her eye is the one most often described by others; the notebooks let her be seen on her own terms.

eyes.name: Raymond George Gosling
eyes.role: PhD student in physics, aged 24–27; first under Wilkins, then from 1951 under Franklin's supervision
eyes.where: The King's basement X-ray room; he set up the cameras and took many of the exposures
eyes.vantage_label: the student at the camera; co-author of the third Nature paper
eyes.form: published papers; interviews and recollections (given later, 1990s–2013)
eyes.authenticity: His contemporaneous record is the joint papers with Franklin and the work notebooks of the unit. His accounts of how Photograph 51 reached Wilkins were given decades later, in interviews and a 2012 published recollection, and are flagged as later testimony. They differ from accounts saying the photograph was shown without Franklin's or Gosling's knowledge.
eyes.bio: Gosling took the first X-ray photograph of a DNA fibre with Wilkins in 1950. Reassigned to Franklin, he worked beside her through the A-form and B-form campaigns and appears with her on the famous 1952 notice mourning the death of the helix. He later had a long career in medical physics. His late interviews made him a key witness to the most disputed hand-over in the story.

sources.title: Gosling's (2012) and Wilkins's accounts of how Photo 51 passed to Wilkins (Memorial University teaching page)
Matt Ridley, 'Raymond Gosling: the forgotten man of the double helix' (2012)

eyes.name: Maurice Hugh Frederick Wilkins
eyes.role: Physicist, aged 34–37; assistant director of Randall's MRC Biophysics Unit, King's College London
eyes.where: King's College London; visited Cambridge to see the model in March 1953
eyes.vantage_label: began the King's DNA work; the go-between to Cambridge
eyes.form: dated letters (to Crick, 1951–1953); published papers; memoir (written later, 2003)
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Crick, including two of 11 December 1951, were among Crick papers found among Sydney Brenner's files and published by Gann and Witkowski in 2010. Others are in his papers at King's College London Archives, digitised by the Wellcome Collection. His autobiography, The Third Man of the Double Helix (2003), was written fifty years later and is flagged as such.
eyes.bio: A New Zealand-born physicist who had worked on uranium isotope separation for the Manhattan Project, Wilkins turned to biophysics after the war. He obtained the first good DNA fibre patterns at King's. He was also Crick's friend, and he had a working relationship with Franklin that broke down almost at once. His letters show a man pulled between loyalty to Randall's unit and his Cambridge friends, and in later life he regretted parts of his own role.

sources.title: Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Archives: DNA Letters, 1951–1953
Papers of M H F Wilkins: correspondence concerning articles in Science, 1969–1970 (Wellcome Collection)
Nobel Prize: Maurice Wilkins

eyes.name: Francis Harry Compton Crick
eyes.role: Physicist turned biologist, aged 35–37; PhD student in Perutz's MRC unit at the Cavendish Laboratory
eyes.side: Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge (MRC Unit for the Study of the Molecular Structure of Biological Systems)
eyes.where: The Cavendish Laboratory, Free School Lane, and his home in Portugal Place, Cambridge
eyes.vantage_label: model-builder and theorist; co-author of the first Nature paper
eyes.form: dated letters; published papers; memoir (written later, 1988)
eyes.authenticity: His letter to his son Michael dated 19 March 1953, seven handwritten pages with diagrams, was sold at Christie's, New York, on 10 April 2013. The joint letter with Watson to Wilkins of 13 December 1951 is at Cold Spring Harbor. What Mad Pursuit (1988) is a later memoir.
eyes.bio: Crick had worked on naval mines during the war and came late to biology. In Cambridge he was writing a doctoral thesis on protein diffraction, and he had helped work out the theory of how a helix diffracts X-rays. He supplied much of the crystallographic reasoning that turned Watson's guesses into a structure, above all the reading of the C2 symmetry in the King's data as a sign of two chains running in opposite directions.

sources.title: Live Science: Bidder pays $6 million for Crick DNA letter (2013)
Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Archives: DNA Letters, 1951–1953

eyes.name: James Dewey Watson
eyes.role: American postdoctoral fellow, aged 23–25, on a National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis fellowship; at the Cavendish from autumn 1951
eyes.where: Cambridge, with trips to King's College London
eyes.vantage_label: model-builder; co-author of the first Nature paper; later memoirist
eyes.authenticity: His letters of 1951 to his fellowship board are at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Archives. The Double Helix (Atheneum, 1968) is a memoir written fifteen years after the events. Its dialogue and scenes are reconstructions, and its portrait of Franklin was contested from the start by Crick, Wilkins, Franklin's family and friends, and later by Anne Sayre's 1975 biography. Entries from it are flagged.
eyes.bio: A Chicago-trained phage geneticist, Watson moved from Copenhagen to Cambridge in 1951 because he believed the structure of DNA would show how genes copy themselves. He was impatient, competitive and unafraid of being wrong, and he brought biological intuition to the partnership. His memoir made the story famous, and it also made it a quarrel.

sources.title: Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Archives: DNA Letters, 1951–1953
Wellcome Collection: Document reproductions used in The Double Helix (JDW/1/6/17)
Scientific American: James Watson dies at 97 (2025)

eyes.name: Linus Carl Pauling
eyes.role: Chemist, aged 51–52; head of the Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology
eyes.where: Pasadena; in Europe in April 1953 (Cambridge, then the Solvay conference in Brussels)
eyes.vantage_label: the rival abroad; working from old, poorer data
eyes.form: research notebooks; dated letters; published paper
eyes.authenticity: His research notebooks, manuscripts and family letters are in the Ava Helen and Linus Pauling Papers at Oregon State University and are digitised in 'Linus Pauling and the Race for DNA: A Documentary History'. Dates here follow the archive's own catalogue.
eyes.bio: Pauling had solved the alpha helix of proteins in 1951 and was the man Cambridge feared. In 1952 the US State Department refused him a passport over his politics, so he never saw the King's photographs. Working from older, poorer pictures, he proposed in a few weeks a three-chain structure with the phosphates packed in the centre. His letters show the speed and confidence that misled him, and the grace with which he accepted the answer.

eyes.name: Peter Jeffress Pauling
eyes.role: Linus Pauling's son, aged 21; research student at the Cavendish, sharing an office with Watson and Crick
eyes.where: The Cavendish office shared with Watson and Crick; travelling on the Continent over the winter break
eyes.vantage_label: inside the rival office, writing home
eyes.authenticity: His letters home are in the Pauling Papers at Oregon State University and are digitised with transcripts. The best-known scene, Peter bringing a copy of his father's manuscript into the office, comes from Watson's later memoir, though the manuscript itself survives.
eyes.bio: Peter Pauling came to Cambridge in 1952 to work under John Kendrew. He was popular, sociable and unconcerned with secrecy. His letters home describe Cambridge gossip, his travels and the King's–Cambridge tensions in a cheerful tone. He was the channel through which Pauling's manuscript reached the very men it would spur on.

eyes.name: Max Ferdinand Perutz
eyes.role: Austrian-born crystallographer, aged 38; head of the MRC unit at the Cavendish and a member of the MRC Biophysics Research Committee
eyes.vantage_label: Crick and Watson's unit head; the man who passed on the MRC report
eyes.form: letter (written later, 1969, to Science) and correspondence
eyes.authenticity: His defence of passing the King's report to Crick and Watson was published as a letter in Science in 1969, after Watson's book appeared. The drafting correspondence with Bragg, Randall and Wilkins (Oct 1968–June 1969) is in Randall's papers at the Churchill Archives Centre (RNDL 2/4). It is later testimony and is flagged.
eyes.bio: A refugee from Vienna who had spent decades on haemoglobin, Perutz sat on the MRC committee that visited King's in December 1952 and received its progress report. He gave a copy to Crick and Watson early in 1953. Once Watson's memoir appeared he was attacked for it, and he answered in print. Colleagues remembered him as a generous team player.

sources.title: Churchill Archives Centre: correspondence about Perutz's letter to Science (RNDL 2/4)
CSHL: Letter from Max Perutz to the Editor of Science (1969)
Nature correspondence: 'History and science united to vindicate Perutz' (2003)

eyes.name: John Turton Randall
eyes.role: Physicist, aged 45–48; Wheatstone Professor of Physics and director of the MRC Biophysics Research Unit, King's College London
eyes.vantage_label: director of the King's unit; set its rules
eyes.authenticity: His letter to Franklin of late 1950 defining her role, the unit's report of December 1952 and his correspondence are in his papers at the Churchill Archives Centre (RNDL). They are administrative records, not a diary.
eyes.bio: Co-inventor of the cavity magnetron that powered wartime radar, Randall built the King's biophysics unit with MRC money after the war. He gave Franklin and Gosling the X-ray work on DNA without making the division clear to Wilkins. He was angry at Cambridge's 1951 incursion, and in 1953 he required Franklin to leave DNA behind when she went to Birkbeck. He is the administrator whose decisions set much of the stage.

sources.title: Churchill Archives Centre: Randall papers, correspondence on Perutz's letter and the MRC report (RNDL 2/4)
NLM Profiles in Science: The DNA Riddle

eyes.name: Alexander Rawson Stokes
eyes.role: Physicist and diffraction theorist, aged 31–33; lecturer in Randall's unit, King's College London
eyes.vantage_label: the theorist who first worked out what a helix should look like
eyes.form: published paper; recollections reported by colleagues
eyes.authenticity: His helix calculation of 1951 was not published by him. It is known from colleagues' accounts and from Wilkins. His contemporaneous record is the 1953 Nature paper with Wilkins and Wilson.
eyes.bio: A former student of Lawrence Bragg, Stokes was asked by Wilkins in 1951 what X-ray pattern a helix would give. He worked out the answer, which involves Bessel functions, and brought a diagram the next day. Cochran, Crick and Vand published the same theory independently in 1952. Colleagues remembered him chiefly for his extreme modesty.

sources.title: Physics Today obituary: Alexander Rawson Stokes
Genome Biology research news on Stokes's death (2003)

eyes.name: Odile Crick (née Speed)
eyes.vantage_label: the artist who drew the structure for the world
eyes.authenticity: Her drawing is the diagram in the Watson–Crick paper, captioned in print as 'purely diagrammatic'. No diary of hers is known; facts of her life come from 2007 obituaries.
eyes.bio: Born in King's Lynn to a French mother, she studied art in Vienna in the 1930s and during the war worked for the Admiralty, listening to German broadcasts and translating captured documents, where she met Crick. Her simple ribbon-and-rods sketch of two chains spiralling round a central axis became the defining picture of DNA.

sources.title: Philadelphia Inquirer obituary: Odile Crick, double-helix artist, 86 (2007)

eyes.name: Aaron Klug
eyes.role: Lithuanian-born, South African-raised structural biologist; Franklin's colleague at Birkbeck from 1954, later her scientific executor
eyes.side: Birkbeck College London; later MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge
eyes.authenticity: Klug inherited Franklin's papers and published close readings of her notebooks in Nature (1968, 1974) and the Journal of Molecular Biology (2004). These are later scholarly analyses by a colleague and friend, and are flagged as such. The notebook dates he gives are cited throughout this chapter.
eyes.bio: Klug joined Franklin at Birkbeck to work on virus structure and became her closest collaborator in her last years. He won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for crystallographic electron microscopy. When Watson's memoir appeared he went back to her notebooks to show, date by date, how far she had got on her own.

sources.title: Klug, 'The discovery of the DNA double helix', J. Mol. Biol. 335 (2004) (copy)
Klug, 'Rosalind Franklin and the double helix', Nature 248 (1974)
Wellcome Collection: Papers of M H F Wilkins relating to Klug's research into DNA history

entries.date_display: Late 1950 (the letter is usually dated 4 December 1950)
entries.headline: A letter that drew the lines no one else saw
entries.digest: Before Franklin arrived, Randall wrote to tell her that the X-ray study of DNA fibres would be hers, with Gosling assisting, and that she and Gosling would for the time being be the only experimental crystallographers on it. Wilkins was not shown the letter. The misunderstanding it created, over whose project DNA was, poisoned relations at King's from the start.
entries.source_note: NLM Profiles in Science, 'The DNA Riddle' (dates the letter Nov 1950); Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004; King's College archive blog (2010).

entries.headline: From Paris carbons to a basement full of DNA
entries.digest: Franklin came from four happy years at the state chemical laboratory in Paris, where she had mastered X-ray diffraction of coals and carbons. At King's she began building an X-ray laboratory around a new fine-focus tube and a humidity-controlled camera. Wilkins was away when she started, and returned to find what he thought was his project under someone else's direction.
entries.source_note: NLM Profiles in Science chronology (1951–1953 at King's); Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004 ('late 1950 / Jan 1951').

entries.headline: Working out, overnight, what a helix would look like
entries.digest: Wilkins asked Stokes what kind of X-ray pattern a helical molecule would give. Stokes worked out that the answer involved Bessel functions and brought a diagram in the next day. The result predicted the cross-shaped pattern later seen so clearly in Photograph 51. He never published it; Cochran, Crick and Vand reached the same theory independently and published in 1952.
entries.source_note: Physics Today obituary of A. R. Stokes; NLM 'The DNA Riddle' (July 1951).

entries.headline: Franklin tells Wilkins the diffraction work is hers
entries.digest: At a meeting in Cambridge, after Wilkins showed DNA patterns hinting at a helix, Franklin told him to go back to his microscopes and leave the X-ray diffraction to her. The exchange is known from both sides' later accounts. It shows how differently they read Randall's division of labour, and the two barely collaborated after it.
entries.source_note: NLM Profiles in Science, 'The DNA Riddle' (July 1951).

entries.headline: Her seminar notes already put the phosphates outside
entries.digest: Franklin spoke to a King's colloquium on her first year's work. Her surviving notes describe two forms of DNA, the dry crystalline A and the wet B, and point to a helical structure, possibly of several chains, with the phosphate groups on the outside, where water could reach them. The talk was careful and data-driven rather than a structure.
entries.source_note: Cobb & Comfort, Nature 616 (2023), on her Nov 1951 seminar notes; NLM 'The DNA Riddle' (quotes her notes on 'a big helix or a smaller helix').

entries.headline: Watson listens without taking notes, and misremembers
entries.digest: Watson came down from Cambridge to hear Franklin and, by his own later account, took no notes. Back in Cambridge he gave Crick a figure for the water content of her samples that was far too low. That mistake sent the pair towards a compact structure with the phosphates in the middle.
entries.source_note: CSHL Archives, 'DNA Letters 1951–1953' (notes Watson misremembered the water-content data); Watson, The Double Helix (1968, memoir written later).

entries.headline: Explaining himself to the fellowship board
entries.digest: Watson wrote a long letter to C. J. Lapp of the National Research Council explaining why he had left Copenhagen for Cambridge without permission. He argued that working out the structure of nucleic acids was the way to understand how genes copy themselves. His fellowship, and his right to stay, depended on the answer.
entries.source_note: CSHL Archives, 'DNA Letters 1951–1953' (Watson to Lapp, 27 Nov 1951; also Watson to Weiss, 14 Nov 1951).

entries.headline: A three-chain model, and an audience from King's
entries.digest: Within days of the colloquium Crick and Watson had built a three-chain helix with the phosphates in the core held together by magnesium ions. They invited the King's group to see it. Franklin, Wilkins, Gosling and others came up by train, and Franklin pointed out that her data showed far more water than the model allowed, and that the phosphates belonged on the outside.
entries.source_note: NLM 'The DNA Riddle' (Nov 1951 visit); CSHL Archives letters; Watson, The Double Helix (memoir, later).

entries.headline: She sees at once the model will not hold
entries.digest: Shown the Cambridge model, Franklin judged that it would not hold together. Her objections were the ones she had given in her talk: too little water, and phosphates in the wrong place. The King's party went home sure that Cambridge had been guessing. Randall was furious.
entries.source_note: NLM 'The DNA Riddle' (Nov 1951).

entries.headline: Two letters to Crick: one official, one anguished
entries.digest: Wilkins wrote to Crick twice on the same day. A formal typed letter, probably approved by Randall, said the King's unit would not continue a joint approach to nucleic acids with Cambridge. A handwritten one, sent privately, described Randall's anger and Wilkins's own failed efforts to mediate. Shortly afterwards the Cavendish director, Sir Lawrence Bragg, agreed that Crick and Watson should leave DNA to King's.
entries.source_note: CSHL Archives, 'DNA Letters 1951–1953' (two letters of 11 Dec 1951); Gann & Witkowski, Nature 2010.

entries.headline: A breezy reply, heavily crossed out
entries.digest: Crick and Watson answered Wilkins together, in a draft much corrected. Its light tone contrasts with Wilkins's distress. The archivists who studied it read it as a sign that the King's group was divided and dysfunctional, and that the Cambridge pair expected to come back to DNA.
entries.source_note: CSHL Archives, 'DNA Letters 1951–1953' (Crick and Watson to Wilkins, 13 Dec 1951).

entries.headline: The A form refuses to look like a helix
entries.digest: A fibre of the crystalline A form gave a strange 'double orientation' pattern, and Franklin began to doubt that the A form was helical at all. She chose to solve it by the slow, rigorous route of Patterson function analysis rather than by building models. Klug later judged that she was never firmly committed to an anti-helical view, only unwilling to assume what she had not shown.
entries.source_note: Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004 (spring 1952); NLM 'The DNA Riddle' (1952).

entries.place: Basement X-ray room, King's College London
entries.headline: Exposure fifty-one: a cross of spots in the mist
entries.digest: Under Franklin's supervision, Gosling made a long exposure of a B-form fibre kept at very high humidity, about 92 per cent, in a camera flushed with hydrogen to cut scatter. The film, numbered 51 in their series, showed a stark X of spots, the signature of a helix, with a strong layer line marking the 3.4 Å spacing between bases. Franklin set it aside while she pursued the A form.
entries.source_note: UKRI MRC archive blog on Photo 51 (May 1952, method, humidity); ASU Embryo Project (6 May 1952); King's College London, 'The story behind Photograph 51'.

entries.date_display: July 1952 (the card is usually dated Friday 18 July)
entries.headline: A black-edged card mourns the 'crystalline helix'
entries.digest: Gosling and Franklin pinned up a mock funeral notice announcing the death of the DNA helix in its crystalline form, and inviting colleagues to a memorial. It was a joke aimed partly at Wilkins and Stokes, but it also recorded her honest conclusion at the time: the A-form data did not yet show a helix. It did not deny that the B form was helical.
entries.source_note: NLM 'The DNA Riddle' (July 1952 notice).

entries.headline: A progress report for the visiting committee
entries.digest: Randall prepared a report on the unit's work for an official visit by the Medical Research Council's Biophysics Research Committee. Franklin's section gave her unit-cell measurements and the C2 space-group symmetry of the A form, and confirmed the 34 Å repeat of the B form. The report was not marked confidential. Who might read it, and how far, became a dispute only years later.
entries.source_note: Cobb & Comfort, Nature 616 (2023) (report prepared 15 Dec 1952); Churchill Archives, RNDL 2/2/2 (copy of report) and RNDL 2/4.

entries.headline: Pauling squeezes three chains around a phosphate core
entries.digest: Pauling's research notes from late 1952 show him fitting three intertwined polynucleotide chains together, with the phosphate groups packed tightly near the axis and the bases pointing outwards. He worked from blurred photographs taken years earlier by William Astbury and from density figures. He did not know about the A and B forms, which had confused the older photographs.
entries.source_note: OSU, 'Linus Pauling and the Race for DNA', research notebook addenda dated 20 Dec 1952 and triple-helix notes (1952a.22).

entries.headline: The triple helix goes off on New Year's Eve
entries.digest: Pauling and Robert Corey sent 'A Proposed Structure for the Nucleic Acids' to the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. It was published in February 1953. Copies went out early to colleagues, including one to Peter in Cambridge. Pauling believed he had the answer.
entries.source_note: OSU chronology, 'Proteins, Passports, and the Prize' (submitted to PNAS 31 Dec; published Feb 1953).

entries.headline: Peter writes home: Cambridge has been warning King's about Father
entries.digest: Back from a winter trip through Belgium and Germany, Peter wrote to his parents and brother with news of the DNA world. He told them that Crick and others had for more than a year been pressing the King's group to work harder, warning that otherwise Linus Pauling would get interested in nucleic acids. The letter shows how far the rivalry was already common talk in Cambridge.
entries.source_note: OSU, Peter Pauling to Linus, Ava Helen and Crellin Pauling, 13 Jan 1953, p. 3 (with transcript).

entries.headline: Patterson maps: two chains running in opposite directions
entries.digest: Franklin's notebook records that her Patterson superposition analysis of the A form pointed to two chains running in opposite directions. Combined with the C2 symmetry she had already reported, this was one of the decisive clues of the whole problem. She reached it by her own methods, at King's, in the same weeks that Pauling's paper was in the post.
entries.source_note: Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004 (19 Jan 1953 notebook entry); NLM 'Lab notes on possible DNA structure' (Jan–Jul 1953).

entries.headline: Father's manuscript arrives, and Watson spots the flaw
entries.digest: Peter brought into the shared office the copy of his father's manuscript sent to him from Pasadena. Watson read it and saw that the phosphate groups were un-ionised, so the structure as drawn would not even be an acid. The Cambridge pair concluded Pauling was wrong. They also feared he would soon find his mistake.
entries.source_note: Watson, The Double Helix (memoir, written later); DNALC, 'Linus Pauling's manuscript describing incorrect triple helix, Peter Pauling'; CSHL Archives letters page (Jan 1953 narrative).

entries.headline: Watson carries Pauling's error to London
entries.digest: Watson went to King's with Pauling's manuscript. In his memoir he describes going into Franklin's room uninvited, being rebuffed when he lectured her on helices, and then talking with Wilkins. Wilkins showed him the B-form pattern. Watson later wrote that the sight of the black cross left him in no doubt that the molecule was a helix, and that on the train home he sketched it from memory and settled on two chains.
entries.source_note: Watson, The Double Helix (1968, memoir, later and contested); date 30 Jan 1953 per King's College archive blog (2010) and Wilkins's account as cited in Watson's Annotated and Illustrated Double Helix (2012).

entries.headline: Wilkins shows Watson the pattern he had just been given
entries.digest: Wilkins later recalled that Gosling had met him in a corridor in January and handed him the B-form pattern, making clear he could keep it. He understood this to mean that the B work was passing to him as Franklin prepared to leave. Wilkins then showed it to Watson. Some have defended this as using material properly in his hands; others hold it should not have been shown without Franklin's consent.
entries.source_note: Wilkins's account as quoted in Watson, The Annotated and Illustrated Double Helix (2012), via Memorial University page; UKRI MRC archive blog; ASU Embryo Project.

entries.headline: Gosling's later account: the negative was Franklin's gift
entries.digest: In a recollection published in 2012, Gosling said that Franklin, due to leave King's in March, decided that the best B-form negative should go to Wilkins as a kind of handover gift, and that he himself carried it to Wilkins's laboratory. On this account the photograph changed hands with her knowledge. Other accounts, including some histories, state the reverse. Both are given here as later testimony.
entries.source_note: Gosling (2012) as reproduced on Memorial University page 'Gosling & Wilkins on Photo 51'; contrast ASU Embryo Project ('without Franklin's or Gosling's knowledge').

entries.headline: Back to the B form, and to counting its chains
entries.digest: With the A-form analysis well advanced, Franklin's notebook turns again to the B form and the question of how many chains it had. She took up the photograph she had set aside months earlier and measured it closely.
entries.source_note: Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004 (10 Feb 1953 notebook entry).

entries.headline: The committee report changes hands
entries.digest: Perutz, who as a member of the MRC Biophysics Research Committee had received the King's progress report, let Crick and Watson see it. When Watson's book revived the episode in 1968–69, Perutz replied in Science. He wrote that the report was not confidential, that he had been inexperienced and casual in administrative matters, and that in hindsight he should have asked Randall first. Others have argued that whatever the label, the data were unpublished and Franklin did not know.
entries.source_note: Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004 (second week of Feb 1953); Cobb & Comfort, Nature 2023 (early 1953); Perutz's 1969 letter to Science (CSHL item 83838) and Churchill Archives RNDL 2/4 (drafting correspondence, 1968–69).

entries.headline: C2 symmetry: Crick reads two antiparallel chains
entries.digest: Reading Franklin's measurements in the report, Crick recognised that the C2 space group meant the molecule had a two-fold axis at right angles to the fibre. That implied two chains running in opposite directions, a type of symmetry he knew well from his own thesis work on haemoglobin. He later said the report mattered chiefly because it confirmed what they were building towards.
entries.source_note: Cobb & Comfort, Nature 2023 (C2 symmetry; Crick's later statement on the report); Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004.

entries.headline: The triple helix appears in print
entries.digest: Pauling and Corey's paper appeared in the February issue of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. In Pasadena they kept adjusting the model through January and February, still assuming the phosphates belonged in the centre.
entries.source_note: OSU chronology, 'Proteins, Passports, and the Prize' (published Feb 1953; adjusted Jan–Feb).

entries.headline: Both forms are two-chain helices, and any sequence fits
entries.digest: On 23 February Franklin's notebook begins to treat the A form as helical. The next day she connects it with the B form: both have two chains, with the phosphates outside. She also noted that the sequence of bases along a chain could be irregular, so any order was possible. What she had not yet found was the specific pairing of bases that held the two chains together.
entries.source_note: Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004 (23 and 24 Feb 1953 notebook entries); Cobb & Comfort, Nature 2023 (late Feb notes).

entries.date_display: Saturday 28 February 1953 (date as given in Watson's memoir)
entries.headline: Cardboard bases click into matching pairs
entries.digest: Watson, waiting for the workshop to make metal bases, cut base shapes from stiff card and shuffled them on his desk. He found that adenine paired with thymine, and guanine with cytosine, gave pairs of exactly the same shape. That explained Chargaff's ratios and made a regular double helix possible. Jerry Donohue, an American chemist sharing the office, had just told him the textbook forms of the bases were wrong. The famous scene of Crick announcing in the Eagle pub that they had found the secret of life comes from Watson's memoir; Crick said he did not remember it.
entries.source_note: Watson, The Double Helix (memoir, later); Watson–Crick 1953 acknowledgment of Donohue; Cambridge Past, Present & Future page on 28 Feb 1953.

entries.headline: The metal model stands complete
entries.digest: With machined plates for the bases, Crick and Watson built a full model of two right-handed antiparallel chains with paired bases inside and sugar-phosphate backbones outside. They checked atom spacings with plumb-line and ruler. The model fitted the King's spacings and Chargaff's ratios.
entries.source_note: NLM 'The DNA Riddle' (early March 1953); Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004.

entries.headline: Pauling to Peter: Franklin insists the phosphates are outside
entries.digest: Writing about his coming flight to London, Pauling told Peter that he still could not make out from Peter's letters and a Watson letter to Delbrück just what the Watson–Crick structure was. He reported that Rosalind Franklin had written to him, convinced the phosphates must be on the outside. He admitted he had assumed all along that they were in the centre. He thought rotating the phosphate groups had solved many of his own model's problems.
entries.source_note: OSU, Linus Pauling to Peter Pauling, 10 March 1953, p. 3; Franklin's notes on the Pauling–Corey paper (NLM, Churchill Archives Folder 1/4).

entries.headline: Wilkins sees the model and takes the news home
entries.digest: Invited to Cambridge, Wilkins saw the model and accepted at once that it was probably right. Back at King's the question became how to publish. The answer agreed was that King's would send its own data papers alongside a short Cambridge note.
entries.source_note: King's College archive blog, 'A potted account of the research on DNA at King's College London' (12 Mar 1953); Gann & Witkowski, Nature 2010 (informal publication arrangements).

entries.headline: Franklin leaves King's for Bernal's Birkbeck
entries.digest: Franklin moved to J. D. Bernal's crystallography department at Birkbeck, where she would turn to viruses. Randall's condition was that she leave DNA to King's, though she was allowed to finish her papers. She went to a happier laboratory, carrying her notebooks and a nearly finished paper on the B form.
entries.source_note: Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004 (14 Mar 1953); King's College archive blog (Feb 1953); NLM chronology (Birkbeck 1953–1958).

entries.headline: A dated draft: the B form is a helix
entries.digest: Franklin and Gosling dated a five-page typescript, 'A Note on Molecular Configuration in Sodium Thymonucleate'. It argues that the B form is a helix with the phosphate groups on the outside, about 20 Å across, probably of two coaxial chains. The date matters: it is one day before the Cambridge manuscript reached King's. It became, with small changes, the third Nature paper.
entries.source_note: NLM Profiles in Science, rough draft dated 17 March 1953 (Churchill Archives, Franklin Papers Folder 1/2); Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004.

entries.headline: The Cambridge manuscript reaches King's
entries.digest: The draft Watson–Crick paper arrived at King's, and Wilkins answered Crick in the friendly, joking style of their correspondence. Over the next fortnight the three manuscripts were coordinated informally by letter. Wilkins decided not to send in a further King's note describing a model by Bruce Fraser, because it compared badly with the Cambridge structure. He later regretted this, since the note showed how far thinking at King's had advanced.
entries.source_note: Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 2004 (manuscript reached King's the day after 17 Mar); Gann & Witkowski, 'The lost correspondence of Francis Crick', Nature 2010, summarised on DNA and Social Responsibility blog (Sept 2010).

entries.headline: Seven pages for a twelve-year-old at boarding school
entries.digest: Crick wrote to his son Michael, then twelve and at boarding school, explaining with sketches how two chains wind round each other and how the bases pair. He told him that one chain could serve as a template for the other, so that the molecule could copy itself, and that this might be how life comes from life. The letter was sold at Christie's, New York, on 10 April 2013 for just over six million dollars including fees.
entries.source_note: Live Science, 'Bidder pays $6 million for Crick DNA letter' (10 April 2013 sale; letter dated 19 March 1953).

entries.headline: An artist draws the structure for print
entries.digest: For the short Nature note, Odile Crick drew the figure: two ribbons spiralling round a vertical axis, joined by horizontal rods for the base pairs. The printed caption calls the figure purely diagrammatic. It became the most reproduced picture of the molecule.
entries.source_note: Philadelphia Inquirer obituary (2007); Watson & Crick, Nature 171 (1953), figure caption.

entries.headline: The note goes to Nature, dated 2 April
entries.digest: The Watson–Crick paper, 'A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid', went to Nature bearing the date 2 April. It was about a page long. It thanked Donohue, and said the authors had been stimulated by knowing the general nature of the unpublished results and ideas of Wilkins, Franklin and their colleagues at King's. It ended with the famous understatement that the pairing suggested a copying mechanism.
entries.quote: It has not escaped our notice
entries.source_note: Watson & Crick, Nature 171:737 (1953), date line and acknowledgments (teaching copy, University of Colorado).

entries.place: Cambridge, on the way to Brussels
entries.headline: Pauling sees the model and concedes
entries.digest: With a passport now allowing him to travel, Pauling stopped in Cambridge on his way to the Solvay conference on proteins in Brussels and saw the model. He accepted it, by every account graciously, and he spoke of it in Brussels.
entries.source_note: OSU chronology, 'Proteins, Passports, and the Prize' (April 1953 visit); OSU Pauling calendar, Brussels, 7 April 1953.

entries.date_display: Friday 17 April 1953 (as given in Gosling's later account)
entries.headline: Randall tells Franklin to stop thinking about DNA
entries.digest: Gosling's later account dates to this week Randall's written instruction that Franklin, now at Birkbeck, should stop working on DNA and leave the problem to King's. She finished her data papers and the July Nature follow-up with Gosling, then turned to tobacco mosaic virus.
entries.source_note: Gosling (2012) as reproduced on Memorial University page; NLM chronology (Birkbeck work on viruses).

entries.headline: Pauling to Delbrück: deeply impressed, and why King's won
entries.digest: Pauling wrote to Max Delbrück that he had been deeply impressed by the Watson–Crick structure, and urged that Watson be allowed time in Cambridge after the summer virus symposium. He explained why his own photographs had been poorer and how the King's group's better results had allowed the double helix to be deduced. He added, without conviction, that the pair might still be wrong.
entries.source_note: OSU Pauling calendar: Linus Pauling to Max Delbrück, 20 April 1953.

entries.headline: Three papers, one after another, in a single issue
entries.digest: Nature printed the Watson–Crick structure, then 'Molecular Structure of Deoxypentose Nucleic Acids' by Wilkins, Stokes and Herbert Wilson, then Franklin and Gosling's 'Molecular Configuration in Sodium Thymonucleate'. The King's papers presented the diffraction theory and data that supported a helix; Franklin and Gosling's printed Photograph 51 as its only figure. Read in order, the issue looked like experimental confirmation of a Cambridge idea. That framing has been questioned ever since, since the data came first.
entries.source_note: Physics Today obituary of Stokes (25 April 1953 papers); ASU Embryo Project on Franklin & Gosling, Nature 171:740.

entries.headline: Her paper appears, with a line fitted to the model
entries.digest: Franklin and Gosling's paper appeared third. Apart from a closing sentence noting that their ideas were not inconsistent with the model in the preceding communication, it was essentially her draft of 17 March. It set out the helix, the outside phosphates, the 20 Å diameter and the likelihood of two chains. In July she and Gosling published evidence that the crystalline A form was also a two-chain helix.
entries.source_note: NLM draft of 17 March 1953 and its description; ASU Embryo Project; NLM 'The DNA Riddle' (July 1953 paper).

entries.headline: Franklin dies at thirty-seven
entries.digest: Franklin died in London of ovarian cancer, diagnosed in the autumn of 1956. She had kept working at Birkbeck on the structure of tobacco mosaic virus, and her group, Klug among them, had located its RNA. Klug carried on the virus work and inherited her papers, including the DNA notebooks.
entries.source_note: NLM Profiles in Science chronology (diagnosis fall 1956; death 16 April 1958; TMV work).

entries.headline: A Nobel Prize for three
entries.digest: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Crick, Watson and Wilkins for their discoveries on the molecular structure of nucleic acids and its significance for information transfer in living material. Franklin had died four years before; the Nobel statutes do not allow posthumous awards. Klug's own Nobel, in chemistry, followed in 1982.
entries.source_note: Nobelprize.org, Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1962 summary (announcement date from the standard record).

entries.headline: The Double Helix: a memoir that started a quarrel
entries.digest: Watson's account appeared after Harvard University Press had withdrawn from publishing it under pressure from Crick and Wilkins, who objected to its portrayal of them. It sold enormously. Its picture of 'Rosy' as a difficult, unhelpful obstacle was attacked as unfair by Franklin's friends and family. In an epilogue Watson praised her later work and admitted his early impressions had been wrong. Every later account of the credit question argues with this book.
entries.source_note: Watson, The Double Helix (Atheneum, 1968); Wellcome Collection JDW/1/6/17; Churchill Archives RNDL 2/4 (responses, 1968–69).

entries.headline: Perutz answers in Science, after months of drafts
entries.digest: From October 1968 Perutz drafted a public answer to Watson's account of the King's report, corresponding with Bragg, Randall and Wilkins. His letter in Science said the report had not been confidential, that he had shared it without thinking, and that he should have asked Randall. Wilkins and Watson also wrote to Science, and the file shows Wilkins objecting to Watson's draft. Later historians, including a 2003 Nature correspondence, largely endorsed Perutz's account of the document's status.
entries.source_note: Churchill Archives RNDL 2/4 (29 Oct 1968 – 5 June 1969); Wellcome Collection, Wilkins papers K/PP178/3/39/6 (Wilkins to Watson, 23 May 1969); CSHL item 83838; Nature 424:127 (2003).

entries.headline: Reading her notebooks against the memoir
entries.digest: Provoked by Watson's book, Klug went through Franklin's notebooks and published what they showed: that by late February 1953 she had two-chain helices with outside phosphates for both forms, and was converging on the structure by her own route. He judged her a step or two from base-pairing, and in 2004 restated that she would have got there more slowly and without the single dramatic paper. His analyses are the main source for the notebook dates used here.
entries.source_note: Klug, Nature 248:787 (1974); Klug, J. Mol. Biol. 335 (2004); Wellcome, Wilkins papers relating to Klug's research.

entries.headline: The student at the camera asks to be remembered
entries.digest: Late in life Gosling gave interviews and a published recollection about the King's years. He described taking the first DNA fibre photograph with Wilkins in 1950 and the long basement exposures with Franklin, and he defended both of them. Some commentators noted that Franklin's overdue recognition had in turn obscured his own share in collecting the data. He died in 2015.
entries.source_note: Matt Ridley blog (16 Dec 2012); Gosling (2012) via Memorial University page.

convergences.label: Franklin's colloquium and the three-chain model
convergences.note: The same talk produced two opposite results. Franklin's notes put the phosphates outside, while Watson, misremembering her water figures, helped build a model with them inside. Within days she was looking at that model in Cambridge and explaining why it could not stand.

convergences.label: The moratorium letters
convergences.note: Wilkins's official and private letters of 11 December, and the Cambridge reply of 13 December, show the same decision from both ends. To Randall it was an incursion stopped. To Wilkins it was a loss of friendship. To Crick and Watson it was a temporary setback.

convergences.label: Pauling's paper and Franklin's Patterson maps
convergences.note: Pauling posted his three-chain structure on New Year's Eve. Less than three weeks later Franklin's notebook showed two antiparallel chains in the A form. Meanwhile Peter's letters were reporting to Pasadena the Cambridge talk about the race.

convergences.label: Photograph 51 changes hands
convergences.note: The most disputed day in the record. Watson's memoir makes it a revelation, and Wilkins describes a pattern lawfully passed to him. Gosling later said it was Franklin's own handover gift, while other histories say she did not know. Her notebook, meanwhile, shows her own analysis already pointing to two chains.

convergences.label: Two routes converge in late February
convergences.note: In the same fortnight Crick read two antiparallel chains in Franklin's C2 data from the report Perutz had passed on, and Franklin wrote that both forms were two-chain helices. Days later Watson found the base pairs. The two groups reached overlapping conclusions independently, by different methods, from the same measurements.

convergences.label: The draft, the manuscript and the letter
convergences.note: Franklin dated her B-form draft on 17 March. The Cambridge paper reached King's on the 18th, and Crick explained the structure to his son on the 19th. Three documents in three days fix the order in which the claims were written down.

convergences.label: Three papers in one issue
convergences.note: The papers were printed one after another, with the model first and the data after. Pauling had just written that the King's data explained why Cambridge had won. The order of the papers, more than any single sentence in them, shaped how credit was seen.

ties.note: Colleagues in the same unit with conflicting ideas of who owned the DNA work, a conflict Randall's letter of late 1950 created and never resolved. They rarely spoke about the science.
Supervisor and PhD student; together they made the A- and B-form photographs and co-authored the third Nature paper.
Close friends since before 1951; Wilkins's letters were the main channel between King's and Cambridge.
Shared an office at the Cavendish and built both the failed and the successful models together.
Father and son; Peter's letters home and his copy of the triple-helix manuscript linked Pasadena to the Cambridge office.
Perutz read Randall's December 1952 report as a committee member and passed it on. In 1968–69 they corresponded about how to account for this in public.
Franklin read the Pauling–Corey paper, listed its errors, and wrote to tell him the phosphates were outside; he reported her letter to Peter on 10 March 1953.
Each worked out the theory of helical diffraction independently in 1951–52: Stokes at King's, unpublished; Crick with Cochran and Vand, in print.
Wife and husband; she drew the figure for his and Watson's paper.
Her colleague at Birkbeck from 1954 and her scientific heir; he later reconstructed her DNA reasoning from her notebooks.
Klug's 1968 and 1974 analyses answered the portrait of Franklin in Watson's memoir with her own dated notebooks.
He heard her colloquium in 1951 and confronted her at King's on 30 January 1953 (by his own later account). After 1953 they were on cordial terms.

threads_out.note: Two of the twentieth century's defining cases about women's credit in science. Marie Curie fought to be named on the work she did with Pierre; Franklin's share was debated after her death, and the Nobel rule against posthumous awards kept her off the 1962 prize. Both stories are now told largely through their own laboratory notebooks.

Franklin spent the war years 1942–46 at the British Coal Utilisation Research Association measuring the porosity of coals for a fuel-short wartime economy. Her coal papers grounded the diffraction skills she brought to DNA. Odile Crick's Admiralty translation work and Francis Crick's naval mine design were wartime jobs too.

Wilkins spent part of the war in Berkeley separating uranium isotopes for the Manhattan Project. He said that unease about the bomb was one reason he turned to biology. He was one of several physicists of the fission generation who moved into biophysics after 1945.

In 1858 Darwin's and Wallace's papers were read together at the Linnean Society; in 1953 three DNA papers were printed one after another in Nature. In both cases the arrangement was made informally by colleagues, and in both it has been debated ever since whether the presentation gave each contributor fair credit.
